organism: Monkeypox virus (MPXV), a double-stranded DNA virus in the Orthopoxvirus genus (the same genus as Variola virus, which caused smallpox, and Vaccinia virus, used in orthopoxvirus vaccines). Two genetically distinct clades circulate: clade I (endemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Central African Republic, Gabon, Republic of the Congo, and part of Cameroon) and clade II (endemic in Nigeria, Cote d'Ivoire, Liberia, Sierra Leone, and part of Cameroon), each further divided into subclades. The animal reservoir is not definitively established, though rodents in the endemic range are suspected. Vaccinia virus and MPXV share more than 90% nucleotide identity, which is why smallpox-era orthopoxvirus vaccines provide cross-protection against mpox.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is 3-17 days (up to 21 in some estimates). Many, though not all, infections begin with a prodrome - fever, malaise, headache, sore throat, cough, and lymphadenopathy (a distinguishing feature from smallpox, which does not typically cause lymph node swelling) - 1-4 days before rash onset; some patients develop the rash first or exclusively. The rash progresses through macular, papular, vesicular, and pustular stages before scabbing and healing, and lesions can be painful or itchy. Since the 2022 clade IIb outbreak, presentation has shifted from the historically diffuse, centrifugal rash toward lesions localized to the genital, anorectal, or oral regions, consistent with the outbreak's predominantly sexual transmission route; lesions may be few in number and easily mistaken for other conditions (e.g. herpes, syphilis). Illness typically resolves within 2-4 weeks. Severe disease and death are more common in young children, pregnant people, and immunocompromised people (especially those with advanced, uncontrolled HIV).
epidemiologySummary: MPXV is zoonotic; the definitive animal reservoir is unknown, but transmission occurs from infected animals to humans in endemic areas. Human-to-human transmission is via direct contact with infectious lesions, scabs, or body fluids (including during sex), respiratory secretions during prolonged close contact, and contaminated fomites (e.g. shared bedding or clothing); transplacental transmission can cause congenital mpox. During the 2022-present clade IIb outbreak, transmission has occurred disproportionately through sexual contact, especially among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM), though anyone with the relevant exposures can be infected regardless of gender or sexual orientation. There is no seasonal pattern. A person is considered infectious from symptom onset (some data suggest possibly earlier) until all lesions have crusted, scabs have fallen off, and a fresh layer of skin has formed.
secularTrendsSummary: The first human mpox case was identified in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1970. The first mpox outbreak outside Africa occurred in the US in 2003 (47 cases across six midwestern states, linked to pet prairie dogs housed with imported small mammals); no US animal-exposure outbreak has recurred since. A global outbreak of clade IIb MPXV beginning in May 2022 - the first to spread extensively via sexual networks, disproportionately affecting MSM - produced roughly 35,000 US cases by 2025 out of about 100,000 cases across 122 countries worldwide, with a global case-fatality rate near 0.2%. US clade IIb case counts stayed relatively stable through 2024 and 2025 at low levels (doubling during September-October 2025 versus the same period in 2024, though still below 2024's overall total), suggesting a transition toward low-level endemic circulation rather than a resolving outbreak. Clade I, historically associated with a much higher case-fatality rate than clade II, caused a separate, larger outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighboring countries starting in 2023-2024 that prompted a WHO Public Health Emergency of International Concern declaration and US preparedness efforts, though sustained clade I transmission has not been established in the US as of this chapter's most recent check.
vaccineDescription: Two orthopoxvirus vaccines are currently licensed in the US. JYNNEOS (MVA-BN, Bavarian Nordic), a live, non-replicating vaccinia virus vaccine licensed in 2019, has been used almost exclusively during the clade IIb outbreak because of its more favorable safety profile and fewer contraindications. ACAM2000, a live, replication-competent vaccinia virus vaccine licensed in 2007 (a descendant of the vaccine used in smallpox eradication), remains licensed but carries a substantially higher risk of serious adverse events, including myopericarditis, and is generally reserved for situations where JYNNEOS isn't available or appropriate. JYNNEOS is given as a 0.5 mL subcutaneous dose (or, under an FDA Emergency Use Authorization adopted as a dose-sparing strategy during vaccine shortages, 0.1 mL intradermally for adults 18 and older); it contains no preservative.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: JYNNEOS is a 2-dose series, with dose 2 given 28 days after dose 1 (as early as 24 days if needed). If the interval is prolonged - even beyond a year - the series does not need to restart; the second dose should simply be given as soon as possible. People who complete the 2-dose series are not currently recommended to receive any additional dose or to be revaccinated during a future outbreak, though data on long-term duration of protection are still accumulating (recent data suggest protection may last more than 5 years). As a non-replicating vaccine, JYNNEOS is managed like an inactivated vaccine for spacing purposes - no minimum interval is required before or after other vaccines - though theoretical concerns about myocarditis mean temporal proximity to a COVID-19 vaccine dose is a consideration some patients may wish to discuss with their provider (see Vaccine Safety).
vaccineEfficacySummary: ACIP's GRADE assessment found moderate-certainty evidence that the 2-dose JYNNEOS series provides some protection against mpox, though basic science data (not captured in the GRADE framework) suggests ACAM2000 would likely be more effective. Real-world vaccine effectiveness estimates from the clade IIb outbreak have ranged from 66% to 89% for the completed 2-dose series. Because JYNNEOS is a whole-virus vaccine that elicits an immune response to many vaccinia proteins rather than a single antigen, effectiveness is not expected to differ meaningfully by MPXV clade, though it may be lower in severely immunocompromised people and can vary by route of exposure and exposure frequency. People who have recovered from a prior mpox infection (either clade) are not recommended to be vaccinated, since natural infection is believed to confer protection; reinfection has been documented in fewer than 0.001% of previously infected US persons through mid-2025, generally milder than the initial infection.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction (e.g. anaphylaxis) to a prior JYNNEOS dose or to any vaccine component is a contraindication. No human safety data exist for JYNNEOS during pregnancy or breastfeeding, but because it is non-replicating, animal studies (rat and rabbit models) have shown no evidence of fetal harm, and it is not withheld from pregnant or lactating people who are otherwise eligible. JYNNEOS has been shown safe and immunogenic in people with well-controlled HIV, atopic dermatitis, eczema, or other exfoliative skin conditions - populations for whom ACAM2000 (a replicating vaccine) would be far riskier or outright contraindicated. Vaccination is not recommended for people who have already recovered from mpox or another orthopoxvirus infection, given the protection natural infection is believed to confer.
vaccineSafetySummary: JYNNEOS has a substantially better safety profile than ACAM2000: ACIP's review found low-certainty evidence of fewer serious adverse events, and specifically fewer cases of myopericarditis, after the JYNNEOS primary series. Myocarditis has nonetheless been associated with JYNNEOS (as it has with some COVID-19 vaccines), so people - particularly males under 40 - considering both vaccines close together in time may wish to discuss spacing with their provider or consult CDC guidance, though no minimum interval is formally required. Adverse events following vaccination should be reported to VAERS, encouraged for any clinically significant event even if causality is uncertain.
vaccineStorageSummary: JYNNEOS may be stored frozen at -25C to -15C (-13F to 5F) until the labeled expiration date, or refrigerated at 2C to 8C (36F to 46F) for up to 8 weeks after thawing; once thawed, it should not be refrozen. See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit, including its mpox-specific addendum, for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Mpox became a nationally notifiable condition on June 23, 2022 (CSTE), and both clade I and clade II infections are reportable in all US states and territories. Laboratory confirmation relies on real-time PCR (or other nucleic acid amplification testing) of lesion material - swabs of vesicle/pustule fluid or roofs, or of dry crusts; serology has limited clinical utility because of cross-reactivity among orthopoxviruses, including from prior smallpox vaccination. See CDC's mpox case definitions and its Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for detailed reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Who Is Currently Recommended for Vaccination
supplementalTopics.summary: For the ongoing clade IIb outbreak, ACIP recommends the 2-dose JYNNEOS series for adults 18 and older at risk for mpox - concretely, sexual partners of MSM with a new diagnosis of one or more sexually transmitted infections, more than one recent sex partner, sex at a commercial sex venue, or sex associated with a large public event in an area with ongoing mpox transmission. MSM without these risk factors (e.g. those in a monogamous relationship) are not part of the recommended population, and eligibility isn't limited to men - anyone with the relevant exposures or behaviors can qualify, and vaccination is not restricted to any particular gender or sexual orientation. Because affirming a specific risk factor can carry stigma, ACIP and CDC advise clinicians to consider vaccinating anyone who requests it (self-attestation) without requiring the patient to specify which criterion applies. Outbreak-specific eligibility can change as an outbreak's epidemiology evolves, since ACIP's recommendation is explicitly tied to the clade IIb outbreak rather than a permanent, standing indication - a future outbreak (e.g. a clade I outbreak with US transmission) could carry a different recommended population.

supplementalTopics.title: Occupational Risk: Health Care Personnel and Laboratorians
supplementalTopics.summary: Separately from outbreak-driven recommendations, ACIP has for decades recommended preexposure JYNNEOS (or ACAM2000) vaccination for people at ongoing occupational risk of orthopoxvirus exposure - chiefly research laboratory personnel who work directly with orthopoxviruses, and some Laboratory Response Network clinical laboratory personnel. For health care personnel who care for mpox patients, or clinical laboratory personnel handling specimens that might contain replication-competent virus during an outbreak, ACIP does NOT routinely recommend vaccination - infection prevention and control practices (e.g. PPE) have proven effective, and occupationally acquired cases have been rare (fewer than 25 among US health care personnel through the clade IIb outbreak, under 0.08% of all cases, and none among laboratorians). Vaccination for these groups is instead offered via shared clinical decision-making, based on site- and activity-specific biosafety risk assessments (e.g. anticipated PPE shortages during a humanitarian mission in a country with endemic mpox).

supplementalTopics.title: JYNNEOS vs. ACAM2000
supplementalTopics.summary: The two licensed orthopoxvirus vaccines differ fundamentally: ACAM2000 is a live, replication-competent vaccinia virus given by multiple-puncture scarification, which produces a visible "take" (a local skin lesion) that itself sheds infectious virus and creates a real transmission and autoinoculation risk to the recipient and their contacts - it is contraindicated in pregnancy, immunocompromise, and several skin conditions (including atopic dermatitis/eczema) for that reason. JYNNEOS, a live but replication-deficient vaccine given as an ordinary injection with no visible take and no viral shedding, avoids essentially all of those contraindications, which is why it has been used almost exclusively during the clade IIb outbreak despite basic science suggesting ACAM2000 may offer somewhat stronger protection. ACAM2000 remains available primarily as a fallback when JYNNEOS is unavailable or inappropriate.

keyPoints: Mpox was first identified in humans in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1970, decades after it was first identified in captive monkeys (1958, the source of its original name)
The 2022 global clade IIb outbreak was the first to spread extensively via sexual contact, disproportionately affecting men who have sex with men, and produced about 35,000 US cases by 2025
Since 2022, rash presentation has shifted toward the genital, anorectal, and oral regions, reflecting the outbreak's predominantly sexual transmission route
A prodrome with lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes) helps distinguish mpox from smallpox, which doesn't typically cause it

JYNNEOS, a non-replicating vaccine with no visible skin "take" and no viral shedding, has replaced the older ACAM2000 as the vaccine of choice because of its far better safety profile in pregnancy, immunocompromise, and skin conditions

Eligibility for vaccination during the clade IIb outbreak is behavior/exposure-based, not gender- or orientation-based - and clinicians are advised to vaccinate anyone who requests it without requiring disclosure of a specific risk factor, given the stigma risk
People who have already had mpox are not recommended to be revaccinated, since natural infection is believed to confer protection and documented reinfection is very rare
Mpox became nationally notifiable in the US in June 2022
